text.title: ASP.NET Core Patterns Core Rules
text.summary: 16 testable rules grounding the ASP.NET Core Patterns methodology, plus the skip rule. Each rule pairs a binary check + sourced rationale. Hard rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: Controllers handle HTTP only: deserialize the request, call exactly one service method, return ActionResult or a typed result. No business logic, no DbContext field, no direct EF Core query in a controller. Services implement an I<X>Service interface and hold the domain logic; repositories expose FindByIdAsync / CreateAsync / UpdateAsync / DeleteAsync and own the queries.
rule.rationale: Direct DbContext access in controllers leaks data-access patterns (N+1, lazy loading), spreads domain logic across the HTTP layer, and makes unit testing impossible without spinning up an HTTP stack. Service isolation gives faster, cleaner tests.

rule.statement: Register DbContext as scoped via services.AddDbContext<T>(...) — never singleton, never transient. Never inject a scoped service (DbContext, scoped repository) into a singleton; a singleton that needs one must resolve it through IServiceProvider.CreateScope(). Reject any diff that puts a DbContext in a singleton constructor.
rule.rationale: DbContext is not thread-safe and each request needs its own instance. A singleton holding a scoped DbContext is a captive dependency: it keeps the context for the process lifetime, causing use-after-dispose and EF state corruption across concurrent requests.

rule.statement: Every async method takes CancellationToken as its last parameter, and every async controller action threads it through the service and repository layers down to the EF Core call: ToListAsync(ct), SaveChangesAsync(ct), FindAsync(id, ct). Never call an async EF Core method without a token.
rule.rationale: Without CancellationToken plumbing, a client disconnect or request timeout does not cancel the in-flight DB query. The client gets a fast timeout while a slow query keeps burning a connection and CPU, and the thread pool starves under load.

rule.statement: All error paths return ProblemDetails (RFC 7807) with a consistent shape { type, title, status, detail, instance }, produced by a global IExceptionHandler (.NET 8+) registered with AddProblemDetails() + UseExceptionHandler(). Ad-hoc error strings, custom error-envelope classes, raw exception messages and stack traces are rejected. Status codes are used correctly: 400 validation shape, 422 validation semantics, 404 not found, 500 server.
rule.rationale: A single machine-readable error contract makes client error handling reliable; without it integrators reverse-engineer a format per endpoint. Custom envelopes diverge per endpoint and break client libraries. Hiding stack traces and SQL errors is also a security property.

rule.statement: DTOs are C# record types with required init properties. Request records carry DataAnnotations or FluentValidation rules; response records carry no logic. Public service methods return DTOs — never a tracked EF entity and never a navigation property. If a client needs related data, add a separate request or a BFF-style aggregation.
rule.rationale: Records give immutability, structural equality and concise syntax; required init guarantees construction-time completeness without mutable setters. Returning tracked entities causes circular JSON serialization, exposes internal columns (HashedPassword), and lets lazy-load exceptions escape past the DbContext scope.

rule.statement: Prefer Mapperly (source-generated) over AutoMapper (reflection-based) for entity↔DTO mapping. Where AutoMapper is already in place, add MapperConfiguration.AssertConfigurationIsValid() to a unit test.
rule.rationale: AutoMapper misconfigurations surface only at request time — an agent adds a DTO property, the compile passes, and production 500s on the first request. Mapperly is AOT-compatible and fails at compile time; AssertConfigurationIsValid() is the equivalent gate for an existing AutoMapper codebase.

rule.statement: Program.cs middleware order is UseExceptionHandler → UseHttpsRedirection → UseAuthentication → UseAuthorization → MapControllers. Never place UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication.
rule.rationale: UseAuthorization checks the ClaimsPrincipal that UseAuthentication sets. Reversed, the principal is always anonymous, [Authorize] is silently skipped, and every endpoint is open with no error to observe.

rule.statement: Configure RequireAuthenticatedUser() as the global fallback policy in Program.cs and opt out per route with [AllowAnonymous]. Every action carries [ProducesResponseType] for each status it can return.
rule.rationale: Agents copy public endpoints into private controllers and forget [Authorize]; a default-authenticated policy converts that omission from a silent exposure into an explicit opt-out that shows up in review.

rule.statement: Inject TimeProvider and call timeProvider.GetUtcNow(); never call DateTime.UtcNow or DateTimeOffset.UtcNow in business logic. Tests inject FakeTimeProvider to drive expiry and scheduling paths.
rule.rationale: DateTime.UtcNow is a static call that cannot be controlled in tests, making time-dependent tests flaky and undebuggable. TimeProvider is the .NET 8 standard abstraction for testable time.

rule.statement: All read-only queries use AsNoTracking(). Tracking is the explicit choice, taken only where the entity will be mutated and saved in the same unit of work.
rule.rationale: Default tracking on a read query builds a change-tracker graph for data nobody will mutate; the memory and CPU cost is a measurable regression at scale. AsNoTracking is the explicit opt-in to the cheap path.

rule.statement: Lazy loading stays off. Load related data explicitly with .Include() / .ThenInclude() in a single query. Never rely on a navigation property materializing on access.
rule.rationale: Lazy loading is convenient in a REPL and a footgun in production: implicit access fires an N+1 storm, or throws use-after-dispose once the DbContext is gone. Eager .Include() makes every query visible in code review.

rule.statement: List endpoints over large tables use keyset pagination (WHERE id > @after ORDER BY id LIMIT 20). Never use Skip/Take on tables above ~100k rows.
rule.rationale: Skip/Take compiles to OFFSET/FETCH, which scans and discards every preceding row — latency degrades linearly with page number, so page 1000 loads 20k rows to throw them away. Keyset ("seek") pagination is O(1) because the database seeks directly to the id boundary.

rule.statement: Wrap multi-step writes in an explicit transaction: await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct); … await tx.CommitAsync(ct);. Never rely on SaveChanges for cross-aggregate atomicity.
rule.rationale: SaveChanges is atomic within one call only. Two SaveChanges calls in the same request are not atomic together — if the second fails, the first is already committed and the database is left partially updated.

rule.statement: Integration tests use WebApplicationFactory<Program> plus Testcontainers Postgres. EF Core InMemory is not used to test real logic.
rule.rationale: InMemory is not relational: it accepts LINQ that never translates to SQL, so tests go green while production goes red. A real database catches N+1 queries, index selection and transaction bugs that InMemory cannot see; WebApplicationFactory exercises the real DI container.

rule.statement: Unit tests use MockBehavior.Strict and assert call counts, or the behaviour is covered by an integration test instead. Reject tests built on MockBehavior.Default that assert nothing about the interaction.
rule.rationale: MockBehavior.Default silently returns default values for unconfigured calls, so a test passes even when production code calls the wrong method or never calls it at all.

rule.statement: One error-handling style per codebase. Reject diffs adding Result<T> wrappers to services in a project that uses exception-based error handling, and the reverse.
rule.rationale: Two styles mean two error paths; every controller must handle both, the global exception handler covers only one of them, and the inconsistency spreads with every new feature.

rule.statement: Skip this methodology when the preconditions in AGENTS.md "Applies If" cannot be met, or when a more specific methodology covers the exact use case better.
rule.rationale: A methodology applied outside its preconditions creates noise; the decision tree routes obvious non-matches to skip rather than forcing a fit.
